name: Beatrice Albright
languages: French (the school insisted, and she reads Colette under the desk)
equipment: Heavy overcoat, camel-coloured, from a Chicago store, with a fur collar she is beginning to be embarrassed by
.32 pocket pistol (Colt 1903, nickel-plated, her late grandfather's), 8 rounds loaded, in her handbag
Press card, Kansas City Monitor, Society and Women's Page, in her hatband where it does not belong
Camera with flashbulbs (a Speed Graphic borrowed from the Monitor's photo desk and not returned)
Portable typewriter, a Remington, at the house on Ward Parkway
A good watch, her grandmother's, and a membership card to the Woman's City Club
Evening clothes, and a good suit she wears on Eighteenth Street so as not to look like she is slumming, which does not work
features: Doors Open (Old Money origin: doormen, maître d's and private secretaries let her through unless told not to; advantage on Society checks among the wealthy; disadvantage on Streetwise checks until she has spent a scene showing she can be trusted or someone vouches for her)

Press Pass (Reporter: crime scenes to the tape, press boxes, courtrooms and corridors are open to her; a source never gets burned through her, and people know it, so she has advantage on Persuasion to get someone to talk off the record)
The Morgue (Reporter: Research takes half the time; once per long rest, one fact the paper has printed about a named person, business or address, with no roll)

Ink by the Barrel (Reporter, 2nd level: when she threatens to print what she knows about someone with a reputation, she may use INT for Intimidation and has advantage; the wrong man remembers, Heat +1)

Beat: Photographer (Reporter, 3rd level: as an action, fire a flashbulb at a creature within 15 ft, CON save DC 13 or blinded until the end of its next turn; her photographs are evidence that police, editors and juries accept)

Family Name (Society Heir background: invitations, tables, audiences with the city's rich and powerful, who assume she is one of them. Her father, the bond lawyer Prescott Albright, does Varnum Bonding's legal work)

personality.traits: I ask one question too many, always, and then apologise for it and ask another. I write in shorthand nobody else can read, including, sometimes, me. I am charming to men who underestimate me, and I keep a list.
personality.ideals: A newspaper should print what is true, especially when it is not what its readers want to hear, and especially when its readers are my parents' friends.
personality.bonds: The Monitor, which hired me for my name and keeps me on the society page for my name, and which I intend to make print my byline on the front page for something else.
personality.flaws: I went to Eighteenth Street on Saturday night with a party of people from the country club to hear 'the colored music', and I sat at a table they would not have let the musicians sit at, and I laughed at somebody's joke about it. I did not know until Monday that I would be ashamed of it for the rest of my life.

appearance: A tall, fair, sharp-featured white woman of twenty-nine with bobbed light-brown hair under a small felt hat, grey eyes that never stop moving, ink on the second finger of her right hand and a camel coat with a fur collar. She has her grandmother's good watch and her father's jaw.
backstory: Beatrice Albright grew up in a stone house on Ward Parkway, the daughter of a bond lawyer and a woman who chairs three charity boards, and was educated at a school in Connecticut that taught her French, posture and how to tell a good pearl from a bad one. She came home in 1930 and talked her way onto the Monitor, the reform evening paper, which was delighted to have an Albright and put her on the society page, where she has written about weddings, debuts and charity balls for six years, with a growing and secret talent for noticing who at the charity ball has just made a great deal of money from the city. On Saturday 24 October she went with a party from the country club to the Gold Leaf Club on Eighteenth Street, and at the next table sat a narrow balding man in a camel coat who listened to the piano player as if the music were the only true thing in the room. She knew his face from the Monitor's files: Virgil Strode, of the Board of Election Commissioners, who has dined at her father's house. On Monday morning she read in the Monitor's police notes, in two lines, that a Negro bandleader was missing from the same club. She does not know yet what she is going to do about it. She knows she is going to do something.
